mappings.note: Matching four liquids to boiling points, explicitly framed as the data needed to judge distillation. LO-10 is the only outcome built on boiling-point differences. Weakish: it is recall of four numbers rather than an explanation, but no other code touches boiling points.

Orders vaporise, condenser, condense, collect for an acetone-water distillation -- LO-10's 'explains distillation'. Not LO-16: this is the internal event sequence of one technique on a two-component mixture, not a plan of successive techniques.

The visible beam is read as evidence of particles big enough to scatter -- LO-15's demonstration clause. Notably the key stops short of naming colloid versus suspension, so the classification outcome LO-14 is not what is being assessed.

Petrol, kerosene and diesel from crude oil is the standard fractional-distillation case, and LO-10 explicitly covers fractional distillation and when it is appropriate. The distractors are the other three techniques, so the judgement is method choice.

Assertion is the under-25-degree condition for fractional distillation, reason is the fractionating column's repeated condensation -- both halves of LO-10's fractional clause. Sits with the other LO-10 items but on the fractional side rather than the simple-distillation side.

Asks for the underlying principle -- differential interaction with solvent and paper -- which is LO-11's 'explains the principle of paper chromatography'. The boiling-point distractor is the LO-10 trap being rejected.

Four candidate mixtures, and simple distillation is picked by testing miscibility and the 25-degree gap -- LO-10's appropriateness clause. The immiscible rows are rejected by that same condition rather than by reasoning about a funnel, so C8.2-LO-11 is not cited.

Three statements all about paper chromatography: what it separates, the solvent-level rule, and the etymology. LO-11. The discriminating statement is the solvent level, which is the same setup rule as item O3 but tested inside a multi-statement stem.

Names mustard oil and water as immiscible. The option set is miscible / immiscible / saturated / colloid, i.e. a liquid-behaviour question, which is the premise LO-11 is built on. Not LO-6: the answer wanted is not 'heterogeneous'.

Which layer sits at the bottom and why -- density, the justification LO-11 asks for. Distinguished from the previous item, which only had to name the immiscibility; here the density ordering is the assessed step.

Three immiscible liquids, and the collection order follows the density stack. Deliberately NOT LO-16 despite three components: LO-16 is about sequencing different techniques and justifying that order, whereas here one funnel is opened once and gravity does the ordering -- still LO-11's density justification.
Definition of sublimation, with deposition offered as the distractor (D). LO-12 covers both terms, so the whole item lives inside it.
The camphor-and-sand bench separation -- LO-12's second clause, 'uses sublimation to separate a suitable solid mixture'. Two components only, so not LO-16.
Definition of deposition, the reverse term LO-12 names alongside sublimation. Condensation and solidification are the distractors, so the assessed point is the no-liquid-phase qualifier.

Two beakers classified as true solution and colloid purely from whether the beam is visible -- LO-15's 'uses it to identify a colloid'. Unlike item O28, this one does commit to the colloid label, but it does so from the light test alone, so LO-14 is not needed.

Why an alloy counts as a homogeneous mixture though its components cannot be separated physically -- LO-6 names alloys as one of its classification cases and owns 'explains why a solution is homogeneous'.

WEAK FIT. Matching brass, bronze and stainless steel to their compositions is recall of alloy recipes; LO-6's alloy clause is the only anchor, and only the fourth row ('uniformly mixed metallic homogeneous mixture') is genuinely classification. The 80/20 figures are quoted, never computed, so not LO-7.

The key characteristic asked for is the over-1000 nm particle size of a suspension, with the under-1 nm solution figure as a distractor -- LO-14's 'uses particle size to distinguish a solution, a suspension and a colloid'.

Three mixtures, three different techniques, one code each: sublimable solid = LO-12, differing solubility of pigments in a moving solvent = C1.2-LO-11, heavy solids in a liquid = centrifugation under LO-13. Exactly at the three-code cap, unlike the part-1 seven-row sweep which had to fall back to competency level.

Mud settling under gravity because suspension particles are large -- the contrast case for LO-14's 'explains why the particles of a colloid do not settle'. Not LO-13: nothing is filtered and no alternative technique is selected, the item stops at the settling behaviour.

The mechanism of centrifugation -- outward force driving denser particles down. LO-13 is the only outcome naming centrifugation. Slight stretch: LO-13 is written as 'selects centrifugation', while this item asks how it works rather than when to choose it.

Picks the case where centrifugation is the right tool (cells from plasma) and rejects chalk-in-water, which filtration would handle -- that rejection is exactly LO-13's 'explains why filtration fails ... selects centrifugation instead'. Closer to LO-13's selection clause than the preceding mechanism item.

Reads a finished chromatogram: the highest spot is the most soluble in the solvent. That solubility-in-solvent reasoning is LO-11's 'basis on which a solvent is chosen', applied to interpret the result rather than to set up the run.

Alum clumping fine mud is coagulation, named outright in LO-13 as the alternative when filtration cannot hold fine suspended particles. Not LO-14: the item is about the remedy, not about sizing the particles.

Four statements on coagulation -- alum in water treatment, paneer from milk, acid coagulants, and a false temperature claim. All sit on LO-13's coagulation clause; paneer is a milk-colloid case but the process asked about is coagulation, not the Tyndall or emulsion content of LO-15.
